text.p: My golf-loving father once told me about a man who was having a such a bad day on the links that he walked down to the lake (which had just swallowed three of his drives) and tossed his whole golf bag into the water.

Dad saw the man stomp toward the parking lot, stop, swear, and return to the lake in an even bigger rage. He waded into the water, retrieved the golf bag where he had stored his car keys. He then re-heaved his bag into the lake and stormed toward his car.

Maybe he should have tried something more fun, such as "3D Ultra MiniGolf" from Sierra On-Line (Windows, $45, 800-757-7707). Here are 18 of the most imaginative miniature golf holes you could ever hope to find. You can play on a lush island with a lighthouse, on the grounds of a haunted house, on the moon, in a volcano crater, even underwater. Nothing's par for this course.

On the other hand, "MiniGolf" has a lot of creative ways to lose your ball as well. You may find it zapped by a laser, snatched by a octopus or buzz-sawed into oblivion. The penalty strokes in this game can really add up.
For most people, of course, that's part of the fun.
Unfortunately, this course has technical hazards that players will have to overcome as well.

Most of the time, the game doesn't let you view the hole from the golfer's point of view, which can make it very difficult to line up a shot. One solution is to activate a short "aiming line" to help you point your putter, but that's not always effective.

Second, you don't have to play "MiniGolf" very long to discover situations where you can barely see the ball because it's tucked way into a corner and the game fails to shift to an appropriate view. On one hole, I could see neither the ball nor the putter. Clicking the mouse in an attempt to knock the ball back into view didn't work -- it just kept adding strokes to my score. The only alternative was to replay the hole.
Finally, on one hole, I tapped the ball over the cup and it wouldn't fall in. I had to hit it eight more times from eight different directions before it would drop down.
Overall, "MiniGolf" is fun. Just be aware that there are times when you'll want to hurl this CD-ROM into a lake.

Because Barney the dinosaur oozes enough sucrose to send a normal person into a diabetic coma, I always figured no parent in his right mind would want to buy a CD-ROM featuring an animated car with the sickeningly sappy name of Putt-Putt.
But parents, there's good news about "Putt-Putt Travels Through Time" (Humongous Entertainment, Windows/Macintosh, $40, http://www.humongous.com).

Sure, the purple roadster with the disembodied eyebrows talks like an overly enthusiastic kid, and the characters are all uniformly warm and friendly and encouraging. But youngsters 3 to 8 love that, and "Putt-Putt" caters to them without driving cynical adults away.

The underlying plot of this adventure game, which is the fourth in the popular "Putt-Putt" series, revolves around a time machine that runs with the help of a coin-operated washing machine. Naturally, something goes wrong. Putt-Putt's dog, homework assignment, lunch box and calculator get swept into the time machine. In order to close the time portal, Putt-Putt must travel to four different eras to retrieve the objects.
Along the way, he meets several friendly dinosaurs, some characters from the Old West, a king who loves awful jokes, and folks living in a Jetsons-like city of the future.

Reading skills aren't usually required and the game does have some real educational value. For example, kids learn basic addition skills when they build a battery. Learning right from left is taught by having Putt-Putt take directions from a dinosaur who needs his back scratched.
A few games are elegantly simple logic puzzles, such as one in which Putt-Putt has to teleport between different platforms by punching the right combination of buttons.

Personally, I like children's products where the humour works on multiple levels, a standard set by the Muppets and Sesame Street. It encourages parents to join their kids as they play. Little of the humour in "Putt-Putt" is like that, except when he goes into the future and finds that the Cartown Library has books such as "A Tailgate of Two Cities," "Gone with the Windscreen," and "1984-by-4."

As with other Humongous games (and unlike a lot of other CD-ROMs for children), the animation is excellent. The game is a little different each time you play, and there are plenty of activities to keep a child occupied for a long time.

My only substantive complaint was that the music in the first section of the game seemed too loud and overbearing. Unfortunately, there is no volume control for the music; you can only toggle it off or on.
The cutsie name may make saccharine-sensitive parents cringe, but "Putt-Putt Travels Through Time" is worth taking for a spin.
(Gene Emery is a columnist who covers science and technology. His Internet address is gene.emery(at)prodigy.com. Any opinions in the column are his alone.)
